PELVIS & PERINEUM__Osteology & Pelvic Wa:
Why this matters: the bony pelvis is a ring that transmits weight from the spine to the legs, protects the pelvic viscera and — in the female — forms the birth canal. Master the inlet/outlet borders, the two key ligaments and the sciatic foramina, and obstetrics, pelvic fractures and the nerves that exit the pelvis all fall into place.
The Bony Pelvis
The hip bone (os coxae)
  • Each hip bone = ilium + ischium + pubis, fused at the acetabulum (triradiate cartilage until ~puberty)
  • The two hip bones join the sacrum posteriorly at the sacroiliac (SI) joints and each other anteriorly at the pubic symphysis
  • This closed pelvic ring transmits body weight from the axial skeleton to the femurs
Greater vs lesser pelvis
  • Greater (false) pelvis — above the pelvic inlet, part of the abdominal cavity (between the iliac wings)
  • Lesser (true) pelvis — below the inlet; contains the pelvic viscera and the birth canal
  • The pelvic inlet (brim) is the boundary between them
Pelvic Inlet & Outlet
Pelvic inlet (brim) — borders
  • Posterior: sacral promontory & ala of the sacrum
  • Lateral: the linea terminalis = arcuate line of the ilium + pectineal line (pecten pubis) of the superior pubic ramus
  • Anterior: the pubic symphysis & pubic crest
Pelvic outlet — borders
  • Posterior: the tip of the coccyx
  • Lateral: the ischial tuberosities
  • Posterolateral: the inferior border of the sacrotuberous ligament
  • Anterior: the pubic arch (inferior pubic rami)
Obstetric diameters. The obstetric conjugate (sacral promontory → most posterosuperior point of the pubic symphysis) is the narrowest fixed inlet diameter and cannot be measured directly; the diagonal conjugate (promontory → inferior symphysis) is measured on vaginal examination and is ~1.5–2 cm longer. (The true/anatomical conjugate, to the superior symphyseal margin, is slightly longer.) The interspinous distance (between the ischial spines) is usually the narrowest part of the whole birth canal.
Male vs Female Pelvis
FeatureMaleFemale
General buildThick, heavyThin, light
Pelvic inletHeart-shapedRounded/oval
Subpubic (pubic) angleNarrow (<70°, V-shaped)Wide (>80°, U-shaped)
Greater sciatic notchNarrow (~70°)Wide (~90°)
Ischial spinesProject inwardsEverted
Overall cavityNarrow & deepWide & shallow
The classic Caldwell–Moloy shapes: gynaecoid (the typical “female” round inlet, best for delivery), android (heart-shaped/male), anthropoid (oval, long AP) and platypelloid (flat, wide transverse).
Ligaments & the Sciatic Foramina
The two key ligaments
  • Sacrospinous ligament — sacrum & coccyx → ischial spine
  • Sacrotuberous ligament — sacrum & coccyx → ischial tuberosity
  • Together they convert the greater & lesser sciatic notches into foramina and resist backward rotation of the sacrum
The two foramina
  • Greater sciatic foramen — the main route out of the pelvis into the gluteal region
  • Lesser sciatic foramen — the route into the perineum; the pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels hook around the ischial spine to re-enter here
Greater sciatic foramen contents
  • Piriformis — the key landmark, dividing the foramen
  • Above piriformis: superior gluteal nerve & vessels
  • Below piriformis: inferior gluteal nerve & vessels, sciatic nerve, posterior femoral cutaneous nerve, nerve to quadratus femoris, pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels, nerve to obturator internus
Lesser sciatic foramen contents
  • Tendon of obturator internus
  • Nerve to obturator internus
  • Pudendal nerve & internal pudendal vessels (re-entering the perineum)
The Pelvic Walls
Lateral wall
  • Obturator internus, covered by obturator fascia, with the obturator membrane closing the obturator foramen
  • The obturator canal (superolaterally) transmits the obturator nerve & vessels to the thigh
Posterior wall
  • The sacrum, coccyx & piriformis muscle
  • The sacral plexus lies on piriformis
The Pelvic Floor (Pelvic Diaphragm)
Muscles
  • Levator ani — the main sheet, in three parts: puborectalis, pubococcygeus & iliococcygeus
  • Coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) — posteriorly, on the sacrospinous ligament
  • Arise from the tendinous arch (a thickening of obturator fascia) between the pubis & ischial spine
  • Innervated by the nerve to levator ani (S3–S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve
Function & openings
  • Supports the pelvic viscera; provides tonic contraction for continence
  • Urogenital hiatus (urethra ± vagina) & anal hiatus (anal canal) pass through it
  • Puborectalis forms a sling maintaining the anorectal angle (~80–90°) — relaxing it opens the angle for defecation
  • The perineal body (central tendon) is the anchoring point where floor & perineal muscles meet
Weakness matters. Stretching/tearing of levator ani (childbirth) or pudendal nerve injury → pelvic organ prolapse and stress incontinence. The perineal body is the key target of an episiotomy and can be torn in an obstetric perineal tear.
Joints of the Pelvis
Sacroiliac joint
  • Part synovial (anterior) + part syndesmosis (posterior interosseous ligament); very strong, little movement
  • Transmits weight from the sacrum to the hip bones; a source of low back/buttock pain (sacroiliitis)
Pubic symphysis & pregnancy
  • Secondary cartilaginous joint (fibrocartilage disc) between the pubic bodies
  • Relaxin in pregnancy loosens the symphysis & SI joints to widen the outlet for delivery (can cause symphysis pubis dysfunction)
🧠 Mnemonics
Levator ani parts — “Pretty Pink Iris”: Puborectalis, Pubococcygeus, Iliococcygeus.
Sacrospinous → spine, sacrotuberous → tuberosity — the ligament names tell you their ischial attachment.
Greater sciatic foramen = exit; lesser = re-entry to the perineum (pudendal nerve hooks around the ischial spine).
Female pelvis — wider subpubic angle, rounder inlet, everted spines (“built for birth”).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Each hip bone = ilium + ischium + pubis, fused at the acetabulum.
Pelvic inlet lateral border = linea terminalis (arcuate line + pectineal line).
Pelvic outlet: coccyx, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligament, pubic arch.
Interspinous (ischial spines) distance = narrowest part of the birth canal.
Sacrospinous → ischial spine; sacrotuberous → ischial tuberosity; they form the sciatic foramina.
Piriformis is the key landmark in the greater sciatic foramen (structures above vs below).
Pelvic floor = levator ani (puborectalis, pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus) + coccygeus.
Puborectalis maintains the anorectal angle for faecal continence.
Pubic symphysis = secondary cartilaginous joint; relaxin loosens it in pregnancy.
PELVIS & PERINEUM__Viscera / Organs:
Why this matters: the true pelvis is packed with viscera in three columns — the urinary (bladder, ureters, urethra), the genital (uterus/tubes/ovaries or prostate/vas/seminal vesicles) and the gut (rectum & anal canal). Know their peritoneal relations, blood supply and the ureter–uterine-artery crossing, and catheterisation, hysterectomy, prostate exams and PR bleeding all make sense.
The Urinary Bladder
Structure
  • A muscular reservoir of detrusor (smooth) muscle; empty it is subperitoneal, behind the pubic symphysis (retropubic space of Retzius)
  • The trigone — a smooth triangular area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice (derived from mesoderm, sensitive to stretch)
  • The apex points forward, connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament (remnant of the urachus)
Sphincters & control
  • Internal urethral sphincter — smooth muscle at the neck (well developed in the male; prevents retrograde ejaculation)
  • External urethral sphincter — skeletal muscle in the deep perineal pouch, under voluntary (pudendal) control
  • Parasympathetic (S2–4, pelvic splanchnics) → detrusor contracts, sphincter relaxes → voiding
  • Sympathetic (L1–2, hypogastric) → detrusor relaxes, internal sphincter contracts → storage/continence
The Ureters in the Pelvis
Course
  • Cross the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, then run down the lateral pelvic wall
  • Turn medially to pierce the bladder wall obliquely (a physiological valve preventing reflux) at the vesicoureteric junction
Three constrictions (stones lodge here)
  • Pelviureteric junction (PUJ) — renal pelvis → ureter
  • Where it crosses the pelvic brim / iliac vessels
  • Vesicoureteric junction (VUJ) — narrowest, entering the bladder
Water under the bridge. In the female, the uterine artery crosses anterior (superior) to the ureter near the cervix (“water [ureter] under the bridge [artery]”). The ureter is therefore at risk of ligation during hysterectomy. In the male the ductus deferens crosses superior to the ureter.
The Urethra
Male urethra (~20 cm, 4 parts)
  • Pre-prostatic (at the neck) → prostatic (widest; receives ejaculatory ducts & prostatic ductules) → membranous (shortest, through the external sphincter — least distensible) → spongy/penile (longest, through the corpus spongiosum)
  • Two curves; the membranous part is torn in pelvic fractures (posterior injury) and by instrumentation, whereas the bulbar (spongy) urethra is the classic site of straddle injury (anterior)
Female urethra (~4 cm)
  • Short & straight, opening into the vestibule anterior to the vaginal orifice
  • Short length → far greater risk of ascending UTIs
The Rectum & Anal Canal
Rectum
  • Continuous with the sigmoid at S3; dilated distal ampulla stores faeces
  • Three transverse (Houston) folds; peritoneum covers the upper third (front & sides), the middle third (front only), and the lower third is subperitoneal
  • Arterial supply: superior rectal (from IMA), middle rectal (internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal)
Anal canal & the pectinate line
  • The pectinate (dentate) line marks the hindgut–proctodeum junction (site of the anal valves)
  • Above: visceral (autonomic) innervation, insensate, superior rectal vein → portal, columnar epithelium — internal haemorrhoids (painless)
  • Below: somatic (inferior rectal/pudendal) innervation, very sensitive, drains to systemic veins, squamous epithelium — external haemorrhoids & fissures (painful)
Female Internal Genitalia
The uterus
  • Parts: fundus, body (cavity) and cervix (projects into the vagina at the fornices)
  • Wall layers: endometrium (mucosa, sheds in menses), myometrium (smooth muscle) and perimetrium (peritoneum)
  • Normal position: anteverted (cervix tips forward on the vagina) & anteflexed (body flexed forward on the cervix)
Tubes & ovaries
  • Uterine (Fallopian) tube: infundibulum (with fimbriae) → ampulla (widest; site of fertilisation & the commonest ectopic) → isthmus → intramural
  • Ovary — suspended by the suspensory ligament (carrying the ovarian vessels) and tethered to the uterus by the ovarian ligament
Blood supply & the ureter. The uterine artery (from the internal iliac) supplies the uterus and, via the vaginal artery, the vagina; it anastomoses with the ovarian artery (from the aorta). It crosses over the ureter — the key hysterectomy hazard.
Pelvic Peritoneum, Ligaments & Pouches
Supporting ligaments
  • Broad ligament — a peritoneal fold draping the uterus, tubes & ovaries (mesometrium/mesosalpinx/mesovarium)
  • Round ligament — from the uterine horn through the deep inguinal ring to the labium majus (a gubernaculum remnant)
  • Uterosacral & transverse cervical (cardinal) ligaments — the true structural supports of the cervix
The peritoneal pouches
  • Vesicouterine pouch — between bladder & uterus
  • Rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) — between uterus & rectum; the lowest point of the peritoneal cavity in the female, where fluid/pus/blood collects (drained/sampled via the posterior fornix)
  • In the male: the rectovesical pouch
Male Internal Genitalia
Prostate
  • A walnut-sized gland below the bladder neck, surrounding the prostatic urethra; secretes ~30% of semen
  • Zones: peripheral (posterior — most cancers; palpable on PR), transitional (periurethral — site of BPH), central
  • Palpated anterior to the rectum on digital rectal exam (median sulcus, two lobes)
Ducts & glands
  • Testis/epididymis → ductus (vas) deferens (ascends in the spermatic cord, through the deep ring, crosses the ureter)
  • The vas joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct, opening into the prostatic urethra
  • Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands lie in the deep perineal pouch, draining into the spongy urethra
Clinical Correlations
Ureteric injury in hysterectomy — the ureter runs under the uterine artery near the cervix; clamp the artery carefully.
Ureteric colic — stones impact at the PUJ, pelvic brim or VUJ; loin-to-groin pain.
BPH (transitional zone) → bladder outflow obstruction; prostate cancer (peripheral zone) → hard, irregular gland with loss of median sulcus on PR.
Ectopic pregnancy — most commonly in the ampulla of the tube; can rupture into the pouch of Douglas.
Culdocentesis — free fluid in the pouch of Douglas is sampled through the posterior vaginal fornix.
Internal vs external haemorrhoids — the pectinate line separates painless (visceral) from painful (somatic).
Suprapubic catheter/cystostomy — a full bladder rises above the pubis, stripping peritoneum, so it can be entered extraperitoneally.
🧠 Mnemonics
Water under the bridge — the ureter (water) runs under the uterine artery (bridge). Injured in hysterectomy.
Bladder control — “S2,3,4 empties the bladder” (parasympathetic = detrusor contracts = voiding); sympathetic stores.
Male urethra parts — Please Please Make Sex: Pre-prostatic, Prostatic, Membranous, Spongy.
Pectinate line — above = autonomic/portal/insensate; below = somatic/systemic/painful.
Uterus normal position — anteverted & anteflexed.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Trigone = between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; sensitive to stretch.
Parasympathetic (S2–4) empties the bladder; sympathetic (L1–2) stores it & closes the internal sphincter.
Ureteric constrictions: PUJ, pelvic brim/iliac vessels, VUJ (narrowest).
Uterine artery crosses OVER the ureter — the hysterectomy hazard.
Male urethra: pre-prostatic, prostatic (widest), membranous (least distensible), spongy (longest).
Fertilisation & the commonest ectopic occur in the ampulla of the uterine tube.
Rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) = lowest point of the female peritoneal cavity.
Prostate: peripheral zone = cancer (PR-palpable); transitional zone = BPH.
Ejaculatory duct = vas deferens + seminal vesicle duct, opening into the prostatic urethra.
Rectal blood supply: superior (IMA), middle (internal iliac), inferior (internal pudendal) rectal arteries.
PELVIS & PERINEUM__Nerves & Autonomics:
Why this matters: the pelvis houses the sacral plexus (somatic power to the lower limb & perineum), the pudendal nerve (the perineum’s workhorse) and the autonomic plexuses that run the bladder, bowel and sexual function. Learn “point & shoot,” the pudendal course around the ischial spine and the pelvic pain line, and continence, erectile physiology and referred pain all fall into place.
The Sacral Plexus
Formation & location
  • Formed by the anterior rami of L4–S4; the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) descends into the pelvis to join the sacral roots
  • Lies on the piriformis muscle on the posterior pelvic wall, anterior to the sacrum
  • Most branches leave through the greater sciatic foramen
Key roots to remember
  • Sciatic nerve — L4–S3 (the largest nerve in the body)
  • Pudendal nerve — S2–S4 (“S2,3,4”)
  • Pelvic splanchnic nerves — S2–S4 (parasympathetic)
NerveRootsSupplies
SciaticL4–S3Hamstrings & all of the leg/foot (via tibial + common fibular)
Superior glutealL4–S1Gluteus medius & minimus, tensor fasciae latae
Inferior glutealL5–S2Gluteus maximus
PudendalS2–S4Perineum & external genitalia (motor & sensory)
Posterior femoral cutaneousS1–S3Skin of the posterior thigh & perineum
Nerve to obturator internusL5–S2Obturator internus & superior gemellus
Nerve to quadratus femorisL4–S1Quadratus femoris & inferior gemellus
Pelvic splanchnicS2–S4Parasympathetic to pelvic viscera & hindgut
The Pudendal Nerve (S2–S4)
Course
  • Leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis)
  • Hooks around the ischial spine / sacrospinous ligament and re-enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen
  • Runs in the pudendal (Alcock’s) canal on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa
Branches & function
  • Inferior rectal nerve — external anal sphincter & perianal skin
  • Perineal nerve — perineal muscles, external urethral sphincter & posterior scrotum/labia
  • Dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris — sensory to the glans
  • The main somatic nerve of the perineum: motor to the pelvic-floor & perineal muscles and both external sphincters, sensory to the external genitalia — continence & sexual sensation
Pudendal nerve block. The nerve can be anaesthetised where it hooks the ischial spine — palpated transvaginally and injected just medial/inferior to it — to provide perineal analgesia for the second stage of labour, instrumental delivery or perineal repair.
The Coccygeal Plexus
Formation
  • A small plexus from S4, S5 & the coccygeal nerve (Co), lying on coccygeus
Supply
  • The anococcygeal nerves — sensation to the skin over the coccyx
  • Motor twigs to coccygeus & part of levator ani
Autonomic Supply — the Big Picture
Sympathetic (T10/T12–L2)
  • Reaches the pelvis via the superior hypogastric plexus (anterior to the sacral promontory — a continuation of the aortic plexus + the L3/L4 sympathetic ganglia)
  • It divides into the right & left hypogastric nerves, descending to the inferior hypogastric plexus
  • Also the sacral splanchnic nerves from the sacral sympathetic trunk (ending at the ganglion impar)
  • Functions: ejaculation, vasoconstriction, internal urethral sphincter contraction (storage)
Parasympathetic (S2–S4)
  • The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes, S2–4) — the ONLY parasympathetic outflow below the head that arises from the sacral cord
  • Synapse in the inferior hypogastric plexus or in the walls of the viscera
  • Some fibres ascend through the inferior & superior hypogastric plexuses to the inferior mesenteric plexus to supply the hindgut (descending/sigmoid colon & rectum)
  • Functions: detrusor contraction (voiding), erection, hindgut & rectal motility
The Hypogastric Plexuses
Superior hypogastric plexus
  • A midline plexus anterior to the sacral promontory / lower aorta
  • Mainly sympathetic (+ visceral afferents); gives the right & left hypogastric nerves
  • At risk in aortic/pelvic surgery → ejaculatory dysfunction
Inferior hypogastric plexus
  • Paired, lying on either side of the rectum (near the cervix/prostate)
  • Formed by the hypogastric nerve (sympathetic) + pelvic splanchnics (parasympathetic) + sacral splanchnics
  • Sends sub-plexuses to each organ — rectal, vesical, prostatic and uterovaginal (Frankenhäuser)
Autonomic Control of Pelvic Function
FunctionParasympathetic (S2–4)Sympathetic (L1–2)
BladderDetrusor contracts → voidingDetrusor relaxes, internal sphincter contracts → storage
Sexual (male)Erection (“Point”)Ejaculation (“Shoot”)
RectumContracts rectal wall, relaxes internal anal sphincter → defecationInhibits motility, contracts internal anal sphincter
Point & Shoot. Parasympathetic = Point (erection); Sympathetic = Shoot (emission/ejaculation). Damage to the parasympathetics (e.g. pelvic surgery) → erectile dysfunction; damage to the sympathetics → failure of emission / retrograde ejaculation.
Visceral Pain & the Pelvic Pain Line
Above the pain line
  • Viscera (or parts) touching the peritoneum — e.g. the fundus/body of the uterus, the upper bladder, the sigmoid
  • Pain follows sympathetic afferents back to T12–L2 → referred to the suprapubic region & lower back
Below the pain line
  • Subperitoneal viscera — e.g. the cervix, bladder neck/trigone, lower rectum
  • Pain follows parasympathetic (pelvic splanchnic) afferents to S2–S4 → referred to the perineum & S2–4 dermatomes (e.g. the perineum in labour)
Clinical Correlations
Pudendal nerve block at the ischial spine — perineal anaesthesia for delivery/instrumental birth.
Pudendal neuralgia (cyclist’s syndrome) — burning perineal pain from compression in Alcock’s canal.
Nerve-sparing prostatectomy — preserving the cavernous nerves (from the inferior hypogastric plexus) protects erectile function.
Retrograde ejaculation — sympathetic damage (e.g. after retroperitoneal surgery) → semen passes into the bladder.
Labour pain — first stage (uterine body/cervix) via T10–L1 & S2–4; second stage (perineum) via the pudendal nerve — the basis of the epidural & pudendal block.
Cauda equina syndrome — S2–4 root compression → saddle anaesthesia, painless retention & bowel/sexual dysfunction (surgical emergency).
🧠 Mnemonics
Point & Shoot — Parasympathetic Points (erection); Sympathetic Shoots (ejaculation).
S2,3,4 — “keep the penis/pelvis off the floor”: the pudendal nerve, pelvic splanchnics and pelvic-floor supply all come from S2–4.
Pudendal path — Exit greater → hook the ischial Spine → enter lesser → Alcock’s canal.
Pain line — above = sympathetic → suprapubic/back; below = parasympathetic → perineum.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Sacral plexus = L4–S4, lying on piriformis; the lumbosacral trunk (L4–L5) links it to the lumbar plexus.
Sciatic nerve = L4–S3; pudendal & pelvic splanchnics = S2–4.
Pudendal nerve: greater sciatic foramen → around the ischial spine → lesser sciatic foramen → Alcock’s canal.
Pudendal block is done at the palpable ischial spine.
Parasympathetic = pelvic splanchnics (S2–4) = voiding, erection, hindgut motility.
Sympathetic = superior hypogastric/hypogastric nerves = storage, ejaculation, vasoconstriction.
Point (parasympathetic) & Shoot (sympathetic).
Inferior hypogastric plexus = hypogastric nerve + pelvic splanchnics, on either side of the rectum.
Pelvic pain line: above → sympathetic (T12–L2); below → parasympathetic (S2–4).
PELVIS & PERINEUM__Vessels & Lymphatics:
Why this matters: the pelvis is supplied chiefly by the internal iliac artery, drained by valveless venous plexuses that link to the vertebral veins, and it channels lymph along the iliac nodes — except the gonads. Learn the internal-iliac branches, Batson’s plexus and where each organ’s lymph goes, and internal-iliac ligation, prostate-cancer spread and the para-aortic drainage of testicular tumours all make sense.
The Internal Iliac Artery
Overview
  • The main blood supply of the pelvis; arises where the common iliac artery bifurcates at the pelvic brim (~L5/S1)
  • Descends into the pelvis and divides into an anterior and a posterior division
  • Four of its branches leave the pelvis; the rest supply the pelvic walls & viscera
Posterior division (3 branches)
  • Iliolumbar artery
  • Lateral sacral artery
  • Superior gluteal artery (the largest branch — exits above piriformis)
  • Mnemonic: “I Love Sex” — Iliolumbar, Lateral sacral, Superior gluteal
Anterior division branchSupplies
Umbilical → superior vesicalSuperior bladder; distal part = medial umbilical ligament
ObturatorMedial thigh (via obturator canal)
Inferior vesical (♂) / vaginal (♀)Bladder base, prostate/seminal vesicles / vagina
Middle rectalRectum (anastomoses with superior & inferior rectal)
Uterine (♀)Uterus, crosses over the ureter; anastomoses with the ovarian artery
Internal pudendalPerineum & external genitalia
Inferior glutealGluteal region (exits below piriformis)
Branches That Exit the Pelvis
Via the greater sciatic foramen
  • Superior gluteal — above piriformis
  • Inferior gluteal — below piriformis
  • Internal pudendal — below piriformis (then re-enters the perineum around the ischial spine)
Via the obturator canal
  • The obturator artery (with the obturator nerve) to the medial thigh
  • An aberrant / accessory obturator artery (~20%) arises from the inferior epigastric — at risk in femoral hernia repair (“corona mortis”)
Other Pelvic Arteries
From the aorta / IMA
  • Gonadal (ovarian/testicular) arteries — from the abdominal aorta (~L2); descend to the gonads
  • Superior rectal artery — the continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery; main supply to the upper rectum
  • Median sacral artery — a small midline aortic branch
Internal pudendal artery
  • The chief artery of the perineum; mirrors the pudendal nerve into Alcock’s canal
  • Branches: inferior rectal, perineal, and the arteries of the penis/clitoris (dorsal & deep) — deep arteries fill the erectile tissue
Arterial Anastomoses
Rectal arterial anastomosis — the superior (IMA), middle & inferior rectal arteries anastomose around the anorectum, giving the rectum a rich collateral supply. (The venous counterpart — superior rectal → portal vs middle/inferior → systemic — is the portosystemic site of rectal varices.)
Uterine–ovarian anastomosis — links the internal iliac & aortic supplies along the broad ligament.
Cruciate / trochanteric anastomosis — gluteal & femoral vessels connect at the hip, preserving limb flow if the internal iliac is ligated.
Because of this rich collateral, the internal iliac artery can be ligated (e.g. for uncontrollable postpartum or pelvic haemorrhage) with the pelvis staying viable.
Venous Drainage & the Pelvic Plexuses
Pelvic venous plexuses
  • Interconnected valveless plexuses around the viscera — rectal, vesical, prostatic, uterine & vaginal
  • They drain mainly into the internal iliac veins → common iliac → IVC
  • The superior rectal vein drains to the portal system (a portosystemic anastomosis → rectal varices)
Gonadal & vertebral connections
  • Right gonadal vein → IVC; left gonadal vein → left renal vein (as in the abdomen)
  • The plexuses connect with the internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson’s) — a valveless route for prostate/pelvic cancer to metastasise to the vertebrae, pelvis & brain
Lymphatic Drainage
The main pathway
  • Most pelvic viscera → internal iliac nodes → common iliac → lateral aortic / lumbar (para-aortic) nodes → lumbar trunks → cisterna chyli/thoracic duct
  • External iliac nodes receive lymph from the lower limb (via inguinal nodes) and deep anterior structures
  • Sacral nodes drain the posterior pelvic wall & rectum
The important exceptions
  • Ovaries, testes & uterine tubes → para-aortic (lumbar) nodes directly, following the gonadal vessels (NOT the inguinal nodes)
  • Superficial perineum, lower vagina, lower anal canal (below the pectinate line), scrotum & vulva → superficial inguinal nodes
  • The pectinate line divides the anal canal: above → internal iliac; below → superficial inguinal
Uterine drainage is multidirectional. The fundus & tubal angle → para-aortic nodes (+ along the round ligament to the superficial inguinal); the body → external iliac; the cervix → internal & external iliac + sacral nodes — important for staging endometrial vs cervical cancer.
Clinical Correlations
Internal iliac ligation — used for intractable pelvic/postpartum haemorrhage; collateral anastomoses keep the pelvis perfused.
Batson’s plexus — explains why prostate cancer classically spreads to the lumbar spine & pelvis (sclerotic bony mets).
Testicular cancer spreads to para-aortic nodes (its embryological origin), NOT the inguinal nodes — a scrotal skin cancer would go to the inguinal nodes.
Rectal varices — portal hypertension dilates the superior–middle/inferior rectal anastomosis.
Corona mortis — an aberrant obturator artery can be torn in pelvic fracture or hernia surgery → brisk bleeding.
Ovarian vein thrombosis — a postpartum cause of flank pain/fever (usually right-sided).
🧠 Mnemonics
Posterior division — “I Love Sex”: Iliolumbar, Lateral sacral, Superior gluteal.
Branches leaving the pelvis — the three gluteal-region arteries (superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, internal pudendal) + the obturator through its canal.
Gonadal lymph → para-aortic — testis/ovary drain to the lumbar nodes, following their vessels (“lymph follows the artery of origin”).
Batson bypasses the IVC — valveless pelvic ↔ vertebral veins carry cancer to the spine.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Internal iliac artery = main pelvic supply, from the common iliac at ~L5/S1; anterior + posterior divisions.
Posterior division = iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal (“I Love Sex”).
Superior gluteal exits above piriformis; inferior gluteal & internal pudendal below it.
Uterine artery (internal iliac) crosses over the ureter and anastomoses with the ovarian artery.
Gonadal arteries arise from the aorta (~L2); superior rectal from the IMA.
Left gonadal vein → left renal vein; right gonadal vein → IVC.
Batson’s vertebral venous plexus = valveless route for prostate cancer to the spine.
Ovaries/testes drain to para-aortic (lumbar) nodes, not inguinal.
Anal canal: above the pectinate line → internal iliac nodes; below → superficial inguinal.
Internal iliac artery can be safely ligated thanks to collateral anastomoses.
